Monoid Theory in Alonzo
A Little Theories Formalization in Simple Type Theory

William M. Farmer Thanks: Address: Department of Computing and Software, McMaster University, 1280 Main Street West, Hamilton, Ontario L8S 4L7, Canada. Email: wmfarmer@mcmaster.ca, yankovsd@mcmaster.ca.    Dennis Y. Zvigelsky11footnotemark: 1
November 13, 2024
Abstract

Alonzo is a practice-oriented classical higher-order logic that extends first-order logic and that admits undefined expressions. Named in honor of Alonzo Church, Alonzo is based on Church’s type theory, Church’s formulation of simple type theory. The little theories method is a method for formalizing mathematical knowledge as a theory graph consisting of theories as nodes and theory morphisms as directed edges. The development of a mathematical topic is done in the “little theory” in the theory graph that has the most convenient level of abstraction and the most convenient vocabulary, and then the definitions and theorems produced in the development are transported, as needed, to other theories via the theory morphisms in the theory graph. The purpose of this paper is to illustrate how a body of mathematical knowledge can be formalized in Alonzo using the little theories method. This is done by formalizing monoid theory — the body of mathematical knowledge about monoids — in Alonzo.

Keywords: formal mathematics, simple type theory, little theories method, monoids, theory graphs, mathematical knowledge management.

MSC classification codes: 03B16, 03B38, 68V20, 68V30.

1 Introduction

Formal mathematics is mathematics done within a formal logic. Formalization is the act of expressing mathematical knowledge in a formal logic. One of the chief benefits of formal mathematics is that a body of mathematical knowledge can be formalized as a precise, rigorous, and highly organized structure. This structure records the relationships between mathematical ideas and the contexts that govern mathematical results. Since it is based on a formal logic, it can be developed and analyzed using software.

An attractive and powerful method for organizing mathematical knowledge is the little theories method [21]. A body of mathematical knowledge is represented in the form of a theory graph [31] consisting of theories as nodes and theory morphisms as directed edges. Each mathematical topic is developed in the “little theory” in the theory graph that has the most convenient level of abstraction and the most convenient vocabulary. Then the definitions and theorems produced in the development are transported, as needed, from this abstract theory to other, usually more concrete, theories in the graph via the theory morphisms in the graph.

The purpose of this paper is to illustrate how a body of mathematical knowledge can be formalized in Alonzo [20], a practice-oriented classical higher-order logic that extends first-order logic, using the little theories method. Named in honor of Alonzo Church, Alonzo is based on Church’s type theory [8], Church’s formulation of simple type theory [17], and is closely related to Peter Andrews’ 𝒬0{\cal Q}_{0} [1] and LUTINS [13, 14, 15], the logic of the IMPS proof assistant [22]. Unlike traditional predicate logics, Alonzo admits partial functions and undefined expressions in accordance with the approach employed in mathematical practice that we call the traditional approach to undefinedness [16]. Since partial functions naturally arise from theory morphisms [15], the little theories method works best with a logic like Alonzo that supports partial functions.

Alonzo has a simple syntax with a formal notation for machines and a compact notation for humans that closely resembles the notation found in mathematical practice. The compact notation is defined by the extensive set of notational definitions and conventions given in [20]. Alonzo has two semantics, one for mathematics based on standard models and one for logic based on Henkin-style general models [28]. By virtue of its syntax and semantics, Alonzo is exceptionally well suited for expressing and reasoning about mathematical ideas and, in particular, mathematical structures.

We have chosen monoid theory — the concepts, properties, and facts about monoids — as a sample body of mathematical knowledge to formalize in Alonzo. A monoid is a mathematical structure consisting of a nonempty set, an associative binary function on the set, and a member of the set that is an identity element with respect to the function. Monoids are abundant in mathematics and computing. Single-object categories are monoids. Groups are monoids in which every element has an inverse. And several algebraic structures, such as rings, fields, Boolean algebras, and vector spaces, contain monoids as substructures.

Since a monoid is a significantly simpler algebraic structure than a group, monoid theory lacks the rich structure of group theory. We are formalizing monoid theory in Alonzo, instead of group theory, since it has just enough structure to adequately illustrate how a body of mathematical knowledge can be formalized in Alonzo. We will see that employing the little theories method in the formalization of monoid theory in Alonzo naturally leads to a robust theory graph.

Alonzo is equipped with a set of mathematical knowledge modules (modules for short) for constructing various kinds of mathematical knowledge units. For example, it has modules for constructing “theories” and “theory morphisms”. A language (or signature) of Alonzo is a pair L=(ℬ,𝒞)L=({\cal B},{\cal C}), where ℬ{\cal B} is a finite set of base types and 𝒞{\cal C} is a set of constants, that specifies a set of expressions. A theory of Alonzo is a pair T=(L,Γ)T=(L,\Gamma) where LL is a language called the language of TT and Γ\Gamma is a set of sentences of LL called the axioms of TT. And a theory morphism from a theory T1T_{1} to a theory T2T_{2} is a mapping of the expressions of T1T_{1} to the expressions of T2T_{2} such that (1) base types are mapped to types and closed quasitypes (expressions that denote sets of values), (2) constants are mapped to closed expressions of appropriate type, and (3) valid sentences are mapped to valid sentences.

Alonzo also has modules for constructing “developments” and “development morphisms”. A theory development (or development for short) of Alonzo is a pair D=(T,Ξ)D=(T,\Xi) where TT is a theory and Ξ\Xi is a (possibly empty) sequence of definitions and theorems presented, respectively, as definition and theorem packages (see [20, Section 11.1]). TT is called the bottom theory of DD, and T′T^{\prime}, the extension of TT obtained by adding the definitions in Ξ\Xi to TT, is called the top theory of DD. We say that DD is a development of TT. A development morphism from a development D1D_{1} to a development D2D_{2} is a mapping from the expressions of D1D_{1} to the expressions of D2D_{2} that restricts to a theory morphism from the bottom theory of D1D_{1} to the bottom theory of D2D_{2} and that uniquely extends to a theory morphism from the top theory of D1D_{1} to the top theory of D2D_{2} (see [20, Section 13.4.1]). Theories and theory morphisms are special cases of developments and development morphisms, respectively, since we identify a theory TT with the trivial development (T,[])(T,[\,]).

The modules for constructing developments and development morphisms provide the means to represent knowledge in the form of a development graph, a richer kind of theory graph, in which the nodes are developments and the directed edges are development morphisms. Alonzo includes modules for transporting definitions and theorems from one development to another via development morphisms. The design of Alonzo’s module system is inspired by the IMPS implementation of the little theories method [21, 22].

Although [20] presents a simple and elegant proof system for Alonzo which is derived from Peter Andrews’ proof system for 𝒬0{\cal Q}_{0} [1], in this paper we validate the definitions and theorems in a development using traditional mathematical proof. In this paper, the proofs are not included in the modules used to construct developments. Instead, they are given separately in Appendix A. Alonzo has not been implemented as a proof assistant. However, since Alonzo is closely related to LUTINS [13, 14, 15], the logic of the IMPS proof assistant [22], Alonzo can be implemented in much the same way that LUTINS is implemented in IMPS.

We produced the formalization of monoid theory with just a minimal amount of software support. We used the set of LaTeX macros and environments for Alonzo given in [19] plus a few macros created specifically for this paper. The macros are for presenting Alonzo types and expressions in both the formal and compact notations. The environments are for presenting Alonzo mathematical knowledge modules. The Alonzo modules are printed in brown color.

Alonzo is fully presented in [20]. Due to space limitations, we cannot duplicate the presentation of Alonzo in this paper. So we assume that the reader is familiar with [20].11 1 The reader should be familiar with the syntax and semantics of Alonzo presented in Chapters 4–5; the proof system for Alonzo presented in Chapter 8 and Appendices A–C; the notational conventions presented in Chapters 4 and 6; the tables of notational definitions found in Chapters 4, 6, 10, and 12; and the various kinds of (mathematical knowledge) modules of Alonzo presented in Chapters 9, 11, and 13. The notational definitions that we need for our formalization of monoids that are not found in [20] are given in Tables 1–3. Table 1 defines new special notation. Table 2 defines several parametric pseudoconstants that serve as polymorphic logical constants (see [20, Section 6.1]). And Table 3 defines several useful abbreviations. The notational definitions introduced in this table have the form

where AA is a name written in uppercase, n≥0n\geq 0, the syntactic variables 𝐁α11,…,𝐁α11\mathbf{B}^{1}_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{B}^{1}_{\alpha_{1}} appear in the expression CC, and the bound variables introduced in CC are chosen so that they are not free in 𝐁α11,…,𝐁α11\mathbf{B}^{1}_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{B}^{1}_{\alpha_{1}}. The name of a (nontrivial) development of a theory named X will be given a name of the form X-nn where nn is a positive integer.

The standard approach to formal mathematics emphasizes certification: (1) mathematics is done with the help of a proof assistant and (2) all details are formally proved and mechanically checked. The formalization of monoid theory presented in this paper exemplifies an alternative approach to formal mathematics [18] that emphasizes communication: (1) proofs are written in a traditional (nonformal) style, (2) the underlying logic is designed to be as close to mathematical practice as possible, (3) mathematical knowledge is organized as a development graph using the little theories method, and (4) supporting software systems do not need a formal proof system and thus are much easier to build and use than proof assistants. The result is an approach in which everything is done within a formal logic except for proofs and the entire development is optimized for communication. We will call the standard approach the certification-oriented approach and the alternative approach the communication-oriented approach.

The paper is organized as follows. Sections 2–9 present developments of theories of monoids, commutative monoids, transformation monoids, monoid actions, monoid homomorphisms, and monoids over real number arithmetic, respectively, plus some supporting developments. These developments have been constructed to be illustrative; they are not intended to be complete in any sense. Sections 2–9 also present various development morphisms that are used to transport definitions and theorems from one development to another. Section 10 shows how our formalization of monoid theory can support a theory of strings. Related work is discussed in Section 11. The paper concludes in Section 12 with a summary and some final remarks. The definitions and theorems of the developments we have constructed are validated by traditional mathematical proofs presented in Appendix A. Appendix B contains some miscellaneous theorems needed for the proofs in Appendix A.

2 Monoids

A monoid is a mathematical structure (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) where mm is a nonempty set of values, ⋅:(m×m)→m\cdot:(m\times m)\rightarrow m is an associative function, and e∈me\in m is an identity element with respect to ⋅\cdot. Mathematics and computing are replete with examples of monoids such as (ℕ,+,0)(\mathbb{N},+,0), (ℕ,∗,1)(\mathbb{N},*,1), and (Σ∗,+⁣+,ϵ)(\Sigma^{*},\mathrel{++},\epsilon) where Σ∗\Sigma^{*} is the set of strings over an alphabet Σ\Sigma, +⁣+\mathrel{++} is string concatenation, and ϵ\epsilon is the empty string.

Let T=(L,Γ)T=(L,\Gamma) be a theory22 2 A theory of Alonzo and related notions are presented in Chapter 9 of [20]. of Alonzo. Consider a tuple

(ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha})

where (1) ζα\zeta_{\alpha} is either a type α\alpha of LL or a closed quasitype 𝐐{α}\mathbf{Q}_{\{\alpha\}} of LL and (2) 𝐅(α×α)→α\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}} and 𝐄α\mathbf{E}_{\alpha} are closed expressions of LL. Let 𝐗o\mathbf{X}_{o} be the sentence

𝖬𝖮𝖭𝖮𝖨𝖣⁡(𝐌{α},𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α),\mathsf{MONOID}(\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}),

where MONOID is the abbreviation introduced by the notational definition given in Table 3 and 𝐌{α}\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}} is U{α}U_{\{\alpha\}} if ζα\zeta_{\alpha} is α\alpha and is 𝐐{α}\mathbf{Q}_{\{\alpha\}} otherwise. If T⊨𝐗oT\vDash\mathbf{X}_{o}, then (ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}) denotes a monoid in TT. Stated more precisely, if T⊨𝐗oT\vDash\mathbf{X}_{o}, then, for all general models MM of TT and all assignments φ∈𝖺𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇⁡(M)\varphi\in\mathsf{assign}(M), (ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}) denotes the monoid

(VφM​(𝐌{α}),VφM​(𝐅(α×α)→α),VφM​(𝐄α)).(V^{M}_{\varphi}(\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}}),V^{M}_{\varphi}(\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}}),V^{M}_{\varphi}(\mathbf{E}_{\alpha})).

Thus we can show that (ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}) denotes a monoid in TT by proving T⊨𝐗oT\vDash\mathbf{X}_{o}. However, we may need general definitions and theorems about monoids to prove properties in TT about the monoid denoted by (ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}). It would be extremely inefficient to state these definitions and prove these theorems in TT since instances of these same definitions and theorems could easily be needed for other triples in TT, as well as in other theories, that denote monoids.

Instead of developing part of a monoid theory in TT, we should apply the little theories method and develop a “little theory” TmonT_{\rm mon} of monoids, separate from TT, that has the most convenient level of abstraction and the most convenient vocabulary for talking about monoids. The general definitions and theorems of monoids can then be introduced in a development33 3 A development of Alonzo and related notions are presented in Chapter 11 of [20]. DmonD_{\rm mon} of TmonT_{\rm mon} in a universal abstract form. When these definitions and theorems are needed in a development DD, a development morphism44 4 A theory morphism and a development morphism of Alonzo are presented in Sections 13.3 and 13.4, respectively, of [20]. from DmonD_{\rm mon} to DD can be created and then used to transport the abstract definitions and theorems in DmonD_{\rm mon} to concrete instances of them in DD. The validity of these concrete definitions and theorems in DD is guaranteed by the fact that the abstract definitions and theorems are valid in the top theory of DmonD_{\rm mon} and the development morphism used to transport them preserves validity.

We can verify that (ζα,𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α)(\zeta_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}) denotes a monoid in TT by simply constructing an appropriate theory morphism Φ\Phi from TmonT_{\rm mon} to TT. As a bonus, we can use Φ\Phi to transport the abstract definitions and theorems in TmonT_{\rm mon} to concrete instances of them in TT (or a development of TT) whenever they are needed. Moreover, we do not have to explicitly prove that 𝐗o\mathbf{X}_{o} is valid in TT; instead, we only need to show that there is an abstract theorem of TmonT_{\rm mon} that Φ\Phi transports to 𝐗o\mathbf{X}_{o}.

3 Transportation of Definitions and Theorems

Let TT be a theory such that T⊨𝐗oT\vDash\mathbf{X}_{o} where 𝐗o\mathbf{X}_{o} is

𝖬𝖮𝖭𝖮𝖨𝖣⁡(𝐌{α},𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α),{\mathsf{MONOID}(\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha})},

and assume that DD is some development of TT (which could be TT itself). We would like to show how the definitions and theorems of the development MON-1 can be transported to DD.55 5 A transportation is presented in Subsection 13.4.2 of [20].

Before considering the general case, we will consider the special case when 𝐌{α}\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}} is U{α}U_{\{\alpha\}}, which denotes the entire domain for the type α\alpha, and 𝐅(α×α)→α\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}} and 𝐄α\mathbf{E}_{\alpha} are constants 𝐜(α×α)→α\mathbf{c}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}} and 𝐝α\mathbf{d}_{\alpha}. We start by defining a theory morphism from MON to TT using a theory translation definition module:

Theory Translation Definition 3.1 (Special MON to TT)

4 Opposite and Set Monoids

For every monoid (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e), there is (1) an associated monoid (m,⋅op,e)(m,\cdot^{\rm op},e), where ⋅op\cdot^{\rm op} is the opposite of ⋅\cdot, called the opposite monoid of (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) and (2) a monoid (𝒫⁡(m),⊙,{e})({\cal P}(m),\odot,\{e\}), where 𝒫⁡(m){\cal P}(m) is the power set of mm and ⊙\odot is the set product on 𝒫⁡(m){\cal P}(m), called the set monoid of (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e).

We will construct a development morphism named MON-to-opposite-monoid from the theory MON to its development MON-1 that maps

(M,⋅(M×M)→M,𝖾)(M,\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}},\mathsf{e})

to

(M,⋅(M×M)→Mop,𝖾).(M,{\cdot^{\rm op}_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}},{\mathsf{e}}).

Then we will be able to use this morphism to transport abstract definitions and theorems about monoids to more concrete definitions and theorems about opposite monoids. Here is the definition of MON-to-opposite-monoid:

Development Translation Definition 4.1 (MON to Op. Monoid)

  • Name: MON-to-opposite-monoid.

  • Source development: MON.

  • Target development: MON-1.

  • Base type mapping:

  1. 1.

    M↦MM\mapsto M.

  • Constant mapping:

  1. 1.

    ⋅(M×M)→M↦⋅op(M×M)→M{\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}}\mapsto{\cdot^{\rm op}_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}}.

  2. 2.

    𝖾M↦𝖾M{\mathsf{e}_{M}}\mapsto{\mathsf{e}_{M}}.

Since MON-to-opposite-monoid is a normal translation, it has no obligations of the first kind by [20, Lemma 13.10] and two obligations of the second kind which are valid in the top theory of MON-1 by [20, Lemma 13.11]. It has two obligations of the third kind corresponding to the two axioms of MON. These two obligations are logically equivalent to Thm7 and Thm8, respectively, in MON-1, and so these two theorems are obviously valid in the top theory of MON-1. Therefore, MON-to-opposite-monoid is a development morphism from MON to MON-1 by the Morphism Theorem [20, Theorem 13.13].

We can now transport Thm1 via MON-to-opposite-monoid to show that opposite monoids are indeed monoids:

  • New target development: MON-2.

Similarly, we will construct a development morphism named MON-to-set-monoid from the theory MON to its development MON-2 that maps

(M,⋅(M×M)→M,𝖾M)(M,{\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}},{\mathsf{e}_{M}})

Then we will be able to use this morphism to transport abstract definitions and theorems about monoids to more concrete definitions and theorems about set monoids. Here is the definition of MON-to-set-monoid:

Since MON-to-set-monoid is a normal translation, it has no obligations of the first kind by [20, Lemma 13.10]. It has two obligations of the second kind. The first one is valid in the top theory of MON-2 by part 4 of Lemma B.2 since ⊙({M}×{M})→{M}{\odot_{{({\{M\}}\times{\{M\}})}\rightarrow{\{M\}}}} beta-reduces by [20, Axiom A4] to a function abstraction which is defined by [20, Axiom A5.11]. The second one is valid in the top theory of MON-2 by part 4 of Lemma B.2 since 𝖤{M}{\mathsf{E}_{\{M\}}} is a function abstraction which is defined by [20, Axiom A5.11]. It has two obligations of the third kind corresponding to the two axioms of MON. These two obligations are Thm9 and Thm10, respectively, in MON-2, and so these two theorems are obviously valid in the top theory of MON-2. Therefore, MON-to-set-monoid is a development morphism from MON to MON-2 by the Morphism Theorem [20, Theorem 13.13].

We can now transport Thm1 via MON-to-set-monoid to show that set monoids are indeed monoids:

5 Commutative Monoids

A monoid (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) is commutative if ⋅\cdot is commutative.

Let 𝐘o\mathbf{Y}_{o} be the formula

COM-MONOID​(𝐌{α},𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α),\textsf{COM-MONOID}(\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}),

where COM-MONOID is the abbreviation introduced by the notational definition given in Table 3. 𝐘o\mathbf{Y}_{o} asserts that (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) is a commutative monoid where mm is a set denoting 𝐌{α}\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}}, ⋅:(m×m)→m\cdot:(m\times m)\rightarrow m is a function denoting 𝐅(α×α)→α\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}}, and ee is an element of mm denoting 𝐄α\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}.

We can define a theory of commutative monoids, named COM-MON, by adding an axiom that says ⋅\cdot is commutative to the theory MON using a theory extension module:

Theory Extension 5.1 (Commutative Monoids)

  • Name: COM-MON.

  • Extends MON.

  • New base types:

  • New constants:

  • New axioms:

    ∀x,y:M.x⋅y=y⋅x{\forall\,x,y:M\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y}}={{y}\mathrel{\cdot}{x}}} (⋅\cdot is commutative).

Then we can develop the theory COM-MON using the following development definition module:

Development Definition 5.2 (Commutative Monoids 1)

  • Name: COM-MON-1.

    x (models of COM-MON define commutative monoids).

  • 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟧\mathsf{Def5}: ≤M→M→o=λx,y:M.∃z:M.x⋅z=y{{\mathsf{\leq}_{{M}\rightarrow{{M}\rightarrow{o}}}}={\lambda\,x,y:M\mathrel{.}\exists\,z:M\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{z}}={y}}} (weak order).

  • 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟣𝟦\mathsf{Thm14}: ∀x:M.x≤x{\forall\,x:M\mathrel{.}{x}\mathrel{\leq}{x}} (reflexivity).

Thm13 states that each model of COM-MON defines a commutative monoid. Def5 defines a weak (nonstrict) order that is a pre-order by Thm14 and Thm15. We could have put Def5, Thm14, and Thm15 in a development of MON since Thm14 and Thm15 do not require that ⋅\cdot is commutative, but we have put these in COM-MON instead since ≤M→M→o{\mathsf{\leq}_{{M}\rightarrow{{M}\rightarrow{o}}}} is more natural for commutative monoids than for noncommutative monoids.

Since COM-MON is an extension of MON, there is an inclusion (i.e., a theory morphism whose mapping is the identity function) from MON to COM-MON. This inclusion is defined by the following theory translation definition module:

Theory Translation Definition 5.3 (MON to COM-MON)

  • Name: MON-to-COM-MON.

  • Source theory: MON.

  • Target theory: COM-MON.

  • Base type mapping:

  1. 1.

    M↦MM\mapsto M.

    𝖾M↦𝖾M{\mathsf{e}_{M}}\mapsto{\mathsf{e}_{M}}.

MON-to-COM-MON is a theory morphism from MON to COM-MON and thus is a development morphism from MON-3 to COM-MON-1. By virtue of this development morphism, the definitions and theorems of MON-3 can be freely transported verbatim to COM-MON-1. In the rest of the paper, when a theory T′T^{\prime} is an extension of a theory TT and DD is a development of TT, we will assume that that the definitions and theorems of DD are accessible in any trivial or nontrivial development of T′T^{\prime} without explicitly transporting them via the inclusion from TT to T′T^{\prime}.

6 Transformation Monoids

A very important type of monoid is a monoid composed of transformations of a set. Let ss be a nonempty set. Then (f,∘,𝗂𝖽)(f,\circ,\mathsf{id}), where ff is a set of (partial or total) functions from ss to ss,

∘:((s→s)×(s→s))→(s→s)\circ:((s\rightarrow s)\times(s\rightarrow s))\rightarrow(s\rightarrow s)

is function composition, and 𝗂𝖽:s→s\mathsf{id}:s\rightarrow s is the identity function, is a transformation monoid on ss if ff is closed under ∘\circ and 𝗂𝖽∈f\mathsf{id}\in f. It is easy to verify that every transformation monoid is a monoid. If ff contains every function in the function space s→ss\rightarrow s, then (f,∘,𝗂𝖽)(f,\circ,\mathsf{id}) is clearly a transformation monoid which is called the full transformation monoid on ss. Let us say that a transformation monoid (f,∘,𝗂𝖽)(f,\circ,\mathsf{id}) is standard if ff contains only total functions. In many developments, nonstandard transformation monoids are ignored, but there is no reason to do that here since Alonzo admits undefined expressions and partial functions.

Consider the following theory ONE-BT of one base type:

Theory Definition 6.1 (One Base Type)

  • Name: ONE-BT.

  • Base types: SS.

  • Constants:

  • Axioms:

This theory is sufficient for defining the notion of a transformation monoid in a development of it, but we must first introduce some general facts about function composition. To do that, we need a theory FUN-COMP with four base types in order to state the associativity theorem for function composition in full generality:

  • Base types: A,B,C,DA,B,C,D.

  • Constants:

  • Axioms:

The theory translation MON-to-ONE-BT is normal so that it has no obligations of the first kind by [20, Lemma 13.10]. It has two obligations of the second kind. These are valid in ONE-BT by part 4 of Lemma B.2 since ∘((S→S)×(S→S))→(S→S)\circ_{{({({S}\rightarrow{S})}\times{({S}\rightarrow{S})})}\rightarrow{({S}\rightarrow{S})}} and 𝗂𝖽S→S\mathsf{id}_{{S}\rightarrow{S}} are function abstractions which are defined by [20, Axiom A5.11]. It has two obligations of the third kind corresponding to the two axioms of MON. The two obligations are Thm18 and Thm19, respectively, in ONE-BT-1, and so these two theorems are obviously valid in the top theory of ONE-BT-1. Therefore, MON-to-ONE-BT is a theory morphism from MON to ONE-BT by the Morphism Theorem [20, Theorem 13.13].

trans-monoid is a predicate that is true when it is applied to a set of functions of S→S{{S}\rightarrow{S}} that forms a transformation monoid. Thm20 says that every transformation monoid — including the full transformation monoid — is a monoid.

7 Monoid Actions

A (left) monoid action is a structure (m,s,⋅,e,𝖺𝖼𝗍)(m,s,\cdot,e,\mathsf{act}) where (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) is a monoid and 𝖺𝖼𝗍:(m×s)→s\mathsf{act}:(m\times s)\rightarrow s is a function such that

(1)​x𝖺𝖼𝗍(y𝖺𝖼𝗍z)=(x⋅y)𝖺𝖼𝗍z(1)\ x\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}(y\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}z)=(x\cdot y)\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}z

for all x,y∈Mx,y\in M and z∈sz\in s and

(2)​e𝖺𝖼𝗍z=z(2)\ e\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}z=z

for all z∈sz\in s. We say in this case that the monoid (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) acts on the set ss by the function 𝖺𝖼𝗍\mathsf{act}.

Let 𝐙o\mathbf{Z}_{o} be the formula

MON-ACTION​(𝐌{α},𝐒{β},𝐅(α×α)→α,𝐄α,𝐆(α×β)→β),\textsf{MON-ACTION}(\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}},\mathbf{S}_{\{\beta\}},\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}_{\alpha},\mathbf{G}_{{({\alpha}\times{\beta})}\rightarrow{\beta}}),

where MON-ACTION is the abbreviation introduced by the notational definition given in Table 3. 𝐙o\mathbf{Z}_{o} asserts that (m,s,⋅,e,𝖺𝖼𝗍)(m,s,\cdot,e,\mathsf{act}) is a monoid action where mm is a set denoting 𝐌{α}\mathbf{M}_{\{\alpha\}}, ss is a set denoting 𝐒{β}\mathbf{S}_{\{\beta\}}, ⋅:(m×m)→m\cdot:(m\times m)\rightarrow m is a function denoting 𝐅(α×α)→α\mathbf{F}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}}, ee is an element of mm denoting 𝐄α\mathbf{E}_{\alpha}, and 𝖺𝖼𝗍:(m×s)→s\mathsf{act}:(m\times s)\rightarrow s is a function denoting 𝐆(α×β)→β\mathbf{G}_{{({\alpha}\times{\beta})}\rightarrow{\beta}}.

    ∀x,y:M,s:S.x𝖺𝖼𝗍(y𝖺𝖼𝗍s)=(x⋅y)𝖺𝖼𝗍s{\forall\,x,y:M,\,s:S\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}{({y}\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}{s})}}={{({x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y})}\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}{s}}}
    x (𝖺𝖼𝗍\mathsf{act} is compatible with ⋅\cdot).

    ∀s:S.𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗍s=s{\forall\,s:S\mathrel{.}{{\mathsf{e}}\mathrel{\mathsf{act}}{s}}={s}} (𝖺𝖼𝗍\mathsf{act} is compatible with 𝖾\mathsf{e}).

Development Definition 7.2 (Monoid Actions 1)

𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟤𝟣\mathsf{Thm21} states that each model of MON-ACTION defines a monoid action. 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟤𝟤\mathsf{Thm22} says that 𝖺𝖼𝗍(M×S)→S\mathsf{act}_{{({M}\times{S})}\rightarrow{S}} is total. 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟩\mathsf{Def7} and 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟪\mathsf{Def8} introduce the concepts of an orbit and a stabilizer. And 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟤𝟥\mathsf{Thm23} states that a stabilizer of a monoid action (m,s,⋅,e,𝖺𝖼𝗍)(m,s,\cdot,e,\mathsf{act}) is a submonoid of the monoid (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e). The power of this machinery — monoid actions with orbits and stabilizers — is low with arbitrary monoids but very high with groups, i.e., monoids in which every element has an inverse.

Monoid actions are common in monoid theory. We will present two important examples of monoid actions. The first is the monoid action (m,m,⋅,e,⋅)(m,m,\cdot,e,\cdot) such that the monoid (m,⋅,e)(m,\cdot,e) acts on the set mm of its elements by its function ⋅\cdot. We formalize this by creating the theory morphism from MON-ACT to MON that maps

(M,S,⋅(M×M)→M,𝐞M,𝖺𝖼𝗍(M×S)→S)(M,S,{\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}},{\mathbf{e}_{M}},{\mathsf{act}_{{({M}\times{S})}\rightarrow{S}}})

to

(M,M,⋅(M×M)→M,𝐞M,⋅(M×M)→M):(M,M,{\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}},{\mathbf{e}_{M}},{\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}}}):

The second example is a standard transformation monoid (f,∘,𝗂𝖽)(f,\circ,\mathsf{id}) on ss acting on ss by the function that applies a transformation to a member of ss. (Note that all the functions in ff are total by virtue of the transformation monoid being standard.) We formalize this example as a theory morphism from MON-ACT to ONE-BT extended with a set constant that denotes a standard transformation monoid. 8 Monoid Homomorphisms

Roughly speaking, a monoid homomorphism is a structure-preserving mapping from one monoid to another.

Let 𝐖o\mathbf{W}_{o} be the formula

MON-HOMOM​(𝐌{α}1,𝐌{β}2,𝐅(α×α)→α1,𝐄α1,𝐅(β×β)→β2,𝐄β2,𝐇α→β),{\textsf{MON-HOMOM}(\mathbf{M}^{1}_{\{\alpha\}},\mathbf{M}^{2}_{\{\beta\}},\mathbf{F}^{1}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}},\mathbf{E}^{1}_{\alpha},\mathbf{F}^{2}_{{({\beta}\times{\beta})}\rightarrow{\beta}},\mathbf{E}^{2}_{\beta},\mathbf{H}_{{\alpha}\rightarrow{\beta}})},

where MON-HOMOM is the abbreviation introduced by the notational definition given in Table 3. 𝐖o\mathbf{W}_{o} asserts that

(m1,m2,⋅1,e1,⋅2,e2,h)(m_{1},m_{2},\cdot_{1},e_{1},\cdot_{2},e_{2},h)

is a structure, where m1m_{1} is a set denoting 𝐌{α}1\mathbf{M}^{1}_{\{\alpha\}}, m2m_{2} is a set denoting 𝐌{α}2\mathbf{M}^{2}_{\{\alpha\}}, ⋅1:(m1×m1)→m1\cdot_{1}:(m_{1}\times m_{1})\rightarrow m_{1} is a function denoting 𝐅(α×α)→α1{\mathbf{F}^{1}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}}}, e1e_{1} is an element of m1m_{1} denoting 𝐄α1{\mathbf{E}^{1}_{\alpha}}, ⋅2:(m2×m2)→m2\cdot_{2}:(m_{2}\times m_{2})\rightarrow m_{2} is a function denoting 𝐅(α×α)→α2{\mathbf{F}^{2}_{{({\alpha}\times{\alpha})}\rightarrow{\alpha}}}, e2e_{2} is an element of m2m_{2} denoting 𝐄α2{\mathbf{E}^{2}_{\alpha}}, and h:m1→m2h:m_{1}\rightarrow m_{2} is a function denoting 𝐇α→β{\mathbf{H}_{{\alpha}\rightarrow{\beta}}}, such that hh is a monoid homomorphism from a monoid (m1,⋅1,e1)(m_{1},\cdot_{1},e_{1}) to a monoid (m2,⋅2,e2)(m_{2},\cdot_{2},e_{2}).

The notion of a monoid homomorphism is captured in the theory MON-HOM:

Theory Definition 8.1 (Monoid Homomorphisms)

  • Name: MON-HOM.

  • Base types: M1,M2M_{1},M_{2}.

  • Constants: ⋅(M1×M1)→M1,𝖾M1,⋅(M2×M2)→M2,𝖾M2,𝗁M1→M2\cdot_{{({M_{1}}\times{M_{1}})}\rightarrow{M_{1}}},\;\mathsf{e}_{M_{1}},\;\cdot_{{({M_{2}}\times{M_{2}})}\rightarrow{M_{2}}},\;\mathsf{e}_{M_{2}},\;\mathsf{h}_{{M_{1}}\rightarrow{M_{2}}}.

  • Axioms:

  1. 1.

    ∀x,y,z:M1.x⋅(y⋅z)=(x⋅y)⋅z{\forall\,x,y,z:M_{1}\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{({y}\mathrel{\cdot}{z})}}={{({x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y})}\mathrel{\cdot}{z}}} (⋅(M1×M1)→M1\cdot_{{({M_{1}}\times{M_{1}})}\rightarrow{M_{1}}} is associative).

  2. 2.

    ∀x:M1.𝖾⋅x=x⋅𝖾=x{\forall\,x:M_{1}\mathrel{.}{{\mathsf{e}}\mathrel{\cdot}{x}}\mathrel{=}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{\mathsf{e}}}\mathrel{=}{x}} (𝖾M1\mathsf{e}_{M_{1}} is an identity element).

  3. 3.

    ∀x,y,z:M2.x⋅(y⋅z)=(x⋅y)⋅z{\forall\,x,y,z:M_{2}\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{({y}\mathrel{\cdot}{z})}}={{({x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y})}\mathrel{\cdot}{z}}} (⋅(M2×M2)→M2\cdot_{{({M_{2}}\times{M_{2}})}\rightarrow{M_{2}}} is associative).

  4. 4.

    ∀x:M2.𝖾⋅x=x⋅𝖾=x{\forall\,x:M_{2}\mathrel{.}{{\mathsf{e}}\mathrel{\cdot}{x}}\mathrel{=}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{\mathsf{e}}}\mathrel{=}{x}} (𝖾M2\mathsf{e}_{M_{2}} is an identity element).

  5. 5.

    ∀x,y:M1.𝗁⁡(x⋅y)=(𝗁​x)⋅(𝗁​y){\forall\,x,y:M_{1}\mathrel{.}{\mathsf{h}\,({x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y})}={{(\mathsf{h}\,x)}\mathrel{\cdot}{(\mathsf{h}\,y)}}} (first homomorphism property).

  6. 6.

    𝗁​𝖾M1=𝖾M2{{\mathsf{h}\,\mathsf{e}_{M_{1}}}={\mathsf{e}_{M_{2}}}} (second homomorphism property).

𝗁M1→M2\mathsf{h}_{{M_{1}}\rightarrow{M_{2}}} denotes a monoid homomorphism from the monoid denoted by

(M1,⋅(M1×M1)→M1,𝖾M1)(M_{1},\cdot_{{({M_{1}}\times{M_{1}})}\rightarrow{M_{1}}},\mathsf{e}_{M_{1}})

to the monoid denoted by

(M2,⋅(M2×M2)→M2,𝖾M2).(M_{2},\cdot_{{({M_{2}}\times{M_{2}})}\rightarrow{M_{2}}},\mathsf{e}_{M_{2}}).

9 Monoids over Real Number Arithmetic

We need machinery concerning real number arithmetic to express some concepts about monoids. For instance, an iterated product operator for monoids involves integers. To formalize these kinds of concepts, we need a theory of monoids that includes real number arithmetic. We present in [20, Chapter 12] COF, a theory of complete ordered fields. COF is categorical in the standard sense (see [20]). That is, it has a single standard model up to isomorphism that defines the structure of real number arithmetic.

We define a theory of monoids over COF by extending COF with the language and axioms of MON:

Theory Extension 9.1 (Monoids over COF)

  • Name: MON-over-COF.

  • Extends COF.

  • New base types: MM.

  • New constants: ⋅(M×M)→M,𝖾M\cdot_{{({M}\times{M})}\rightarrow{M}},\;\mathsf{e}_{M}.

  • New axioms:

  1. 19.

    ∀x,y,z:M.x⋅(y⋅z)=(x⋅y)⋅z{\forall\,x,y,z:M\mathrel{.}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{({y}\mathrel{\cdot}{z})}}={{({x}\mathrel{\cdot}{y})}\mathrel{\cdot}{z}}} (⋅\cdot is associative).

  2. 20.

    ∀x:M.𝖾⋅x=x⋅𝖾=x{\forall\,x:M\mathrel{.}{{\mathsf{e}}\mathrel{\cdot}{x}}\mathrel{=}{{x}\mathrel{\cdot}{\mathsf{e}}}\mathrel{=}{x}} (𝖾\mathsf{e} is an identity element).

We can now define an iterated product operator for monoids in a development of MON-over-COF-1:

  • Name: MON-over-COF-1.

  • Definitions and theorems:

  • 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟫\mathsf{Def9}: 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝖽R→R→(R→M)→M={{\mathsf{prod}_{{R}\rightarrow{{R}\rightarrow{{({R}\rightarrow{M})}\rightarrow{M}}}}}={}}

       ∀m,n:Z{R},g:Z{R}→M.f​m​n​g≃{\forall\,m,n:Z_{\{R\}},\,g:{Z_{\{R\}}}\rightarrow{M}\mathrel{.}{f\,m\,n\,g}\simeq{}}
       (m>n↦𝖾∣(f​m​(n-1)​g)⋅(g​n)){({m}\mathrel{>}{n}\mapsto\mathsf{e}\mid{(f\,m\,({n}\mathrel{-}{1})\,g)}\mathrel{\cdot}{(g\,n)})} (iterated product).

  • 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟤𝟫\mathsf{Thm29}: ∀m:Z{R},g:Z{R}→M.(∏i=mmg​i)≃g​m{\forall\,m:Z_{\{R\}},\,g:{Z_{\{R\}}}\rightarrow{M}\mathrel{.}{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{m}{g\,i}\Big)}\simeq{g\,m}}
    x (trivial product).

for the iterated product defined in Table 1.

10 Monoid Theory Applied to Strings

In this section we will show how we can apply the machinery of our monoid theory formalization to a theory of strings over an abstract alphabet. A string over an alphabet AA is a finite sequence of values from AA. The finite sequence ss can be represented as a partial function s:ℕ→As:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow A such that, for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, s⁡(m)s(m) is defined iff m<nm<n.

In [20, Chapter 10] we introduce compact notation for finite (and infinite) sequences represented in this manner. The notation requires a system of natural numbers as defined in [20]. The development COF-dev-2 of the theory COF presented in [20, Chapter 12] includes a system of natural numbers. Therefore, we can define a theory of strings as an extension of COF plus a base type AA that represents an abstract alphabet:

Theory Extension 10.1 (Strings)

  • Name: STR.

  • Extends COF.

  • New base types: AA.

  • New constants:

  • New axioms:

Since STR is an extension of COF, we can assume that STR-1 is a development of STR that contains the 7 definitions of COF-dev-2 named as COF-Def1, …, COF-Def7 and the 22 theorems of COF-dev-2 named as COF-Thm1, …, COF-Thm22.         ∀x:𝗌𝗍𝗋.f⁡(ϵ,x)=x∧{{\forall\,x:\mathsf{str}\mathrel{.}{f\,(\epsilon,x)}={x}}\wedge{}}

MON-over-COF-to-STR-2 has one obligation of the first kind for the mapped base type MM, which is clearly valid since 𝗌𝗍𝗋{R→A}\mathsf{str}_{\{{R}\rightarrow{A}\}} is nonempty. MON-over-COF-to-STR-2 has 12 obligations of the second kind for the 12 mapped constants. The first 10 are trivially valid. The last 2 are valid by 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟣𝟤\mathsf{Def12} and 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟣𝟣\mathsf{Def11}, respectively. And MON-over-COF-to-STR-2 has 20 obligations of the third kind for the 20 axioms of MON-over-COF. The first 18 are trivially valid. The last 2 are valid by 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟥𝟦\mathsf{Thm34} and 𝖳𝗁𝗆𝟥𝟥\mathsf{Thm33}, respectively. Therefore, MON-over-COF-to-STR-2 is a development morphism from the theory MON-over-COF to the development STR-2 by the Morphism Theorem [20, Theorem 13.13].

11 Related Work

As we have seen, a theory (or development) graph provides an effective architecture for formalizing a body of mathematical knowledge. It is especially useful for creating a large library of formal mathematical knowledge that, by necessity, must be constructed in parallel by multiple developers. The library is built in parts by separate development teams and then the parts are linked together by morphisms. Mathematical knowledge is organized as a theory graph in several proof assistants and logical frameworks including Ergo [35], IMPS [21], Isabelle [5], LF [44], MMT [43], and PVS [38]. Theory graphs are also employed in several software specification and development systems including ASL [47], CASL [3, 4], EHDM [45], Hets [32], IOTA [33], KIDS [48], OBJ [24], and Specware [49].

Simple type theory in the form of Church’s type theory is a popular logic for formal mathematics. There are several proof assistants that implement versions of Church’s type theory including HOL [26], HOL Light [27], IMPS [22], Isabelle/HOL [39], ProofPower [42], PVS [37], and TPS [2]. As we mentioned in Section 1, the IMPS proof assistant is especially noteworthy here since it implements LUTINS [13, 14, 15], a version of Church’s type theory that admits undefined expressions and is closely related to Alonzo.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in formalizing mathematics within dependent logics. Several proof assistants and programming languages are based on versions of dependent type theory including Agda [7, 36], Automath [34], Coq [50], Epigram [11], F∗{\rm F}^{\ast} [12], Idris [29], Lean [10], and Nuprl [9]. So which type theory is better for formal mathematics, simple type theory or dependent type theory? This question has become hotly contested. We hope that the reader will see our formalization of monoid theory in Alonzo as evidence for the efficacy of simple type theory as a logical basis for formal mathematics. The reader might also be interested in looking at these recent papers that advocate for simple type theory: [6, 40, 41].

Since monoid theory is a relatively simple subject, there have not been many attempts to formalize it by itself, but there have been several formalizations of group theory. Here are some examples: [23, 25, 30, 46, 51, 52].

12 Conclusion

The developments and development morphisms presented in Sections 2–10 form the development graph GmonG_{\rm mon} shown in Figure 1. The development graph shows all the development morphisms that we have explicitly defined as well as all inclusions corresponding to theory extensions we have explicitly defined. A development morphism that is an inclusion is designated by a ↪\hookrightarrow arrow and a noninclusion is designated by a →\rightarrow arrow. There are many, many more useful development morphisms that are not shown in GmonG_{\rm mon}, including implicit inclusions and a vast number of development morphisms into the theory COF.

The construction of GmonG_{\rm mon} illustrates how a body of mathematical knowledge can be formalized in Alonzo as a development graph in accordance with the little theories method. GmonG_{\rm mon} could be extended to include other mathematical concepts related to monoids such as categories. It could be incorporated in a development graph that formalizes a more extensive body of mathematical knowledge. And it could also be used as a foundation for building a formalization of group theory. This would be done by lifting each development DD of a theory TT that extends MON to a development D′D^{\prime} of a theory T′T^{\prime} that extends a theory GRP obtained by adding an inverse operation to MON. The lifting of DD to D′D^{\prime} would include constructing inclusions from MON to GRP and from TT to T′T^{\prime}.

The formalization of monoid theory we have presented demonstrates three things. First, it demonstrates the power of the little theories method. The formalization is largely free of redundancy since each mathematical topic is articulated in just one development DD, the development for the little theory that is optimal for the topic in level of abstraction and choice of vocabulary. If we create a translation Φ\Phi from DD to another development D′D^{\prime} and prove that Φ\Phi is a morphism, then we can freely transport the definitions and theorems of DD to D′D^{\prime} via Φ\Phi. That is, an abstract concept or fact that has been validated in DD can be translated to a concrete instance of the concept or fact that is automatically validated in D′D^{\prime} provided the translation is a morphism. (This is illustrated by our use of the development morphism MON-over-COF-to-STR-2 to transport definitions and theorems about monoids to a development about strings.) As the result, the same concept or fact can appear in many places in the theory graph but under different assumptions and involving different vocabulary. (For example, the notion of a submonoid represented by the constant 𝗌𝗎𝖻𝗆𝗈𝗇𝗈𝗂𝖽{M}→o{\mathsf{submonoid}_{{\{M\}}\rightarrow{o}}} defined in MON-1 appears in ONE-BT-2 as the notion of a transformation monoid represented by the constant trans-monoid{S→S}→o{\textsf{trans-monoid}_{{\{{S}\rightarrow{S}\}}\rightarrow{o}}}.)

Second, the formalization demonstrates that Alonzo is well suited for expressing and reasoning about mathematical ideas. The simple type theory machinery of Alonzo — function and product types, function application and abstraction, definite description, and ordered pairs — enables mathematical expressions to be formulated in a direct and natural manner. It also enables almost every single mathematical structure or set of mathematical structures to be specified by an Alonzo development. (For example, the development ONE-BT-2 specifies the set of structures consisting of a set SS and the set S→SS\rightarrow S of transformations on SS.) The admission of undefined expressions in Alonzo enables statements involving partial and total functions and definite descriptions to be expressed directly, naturally, and succinctly. (For example, if M=(m,⋅,e)M=(m,\cdot,e) is a monoid, the operation that makes a submonoid m′⊆mm^{\prime}\subseteq m of MM a monoid itself is exactly what is expected: the partial function that results from restricting ⋅\cdot to m′×m′m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}.) And the notational definitions and conventions employed in Alonzo enables mathematical expressions to be presented with the same notation that is used mathematical practice. (For example, Thm33: ∀x:𝗌𝗍𝗋.ϵ​x=x​ϵ=x{\forall\,x:\mathsf{str}\mathrel{.}{{\epsilon}{x}}\mathrel{=}{{x}{\epsilon}}\mathrel{=}{x}}, that states ϵ\epsilon is an identity element for concatenation, is written just as one would expect it to be written in mathematical practice.)

Third, the formalization demonstrates that the communication-oriented approach to formal mathematics (with traditional proofs) has two advantages over the certification-oriented approach (with formal proofs): (1) communication is more effective and (2) formalization is easier. (These two approaches are defined in Section 1.) The certification-oriented approach is done with the help of a proof assistant and all proofs are formal and mechanically checked. Proof assistants are consequently very complex and notoriously difficult to learn how to use. Traditional proofs are easier to read and write than formal proofs and are better suited for communicating the ideas behind proofs. Moreover, since the communication-oriented approach does not require a facility for developing and checking formal proofs, it can be done with software support that is much simpler and easier to use than a proof assistant. (In this paper, our software support was just a set of LaTeX macros and environments.)

The great majority of mathematics practitioners — including mathematicians — are much more interested in communicating mathematical ideas than in formally certifying mathematical results. Hence, the communication-oriented approach is likely to serve the needs of the average mathematics practitioner much better than the certification-oriented approach. This is especially true when the mathematical knowledge involved is well understood (such as monoid theory) and certification via traditional proof is adequate for the purpose at hand.

Appendix A Validation of Definitions and Theorems

Let D=(T,Ξ)D=(T,\Xi) be a development where TT is the bottom theory of the development and Ξ=[P1,…,Pn]\Xi=[P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}] is the list of definition and theorem packages of the development. For each ii with 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, PiP_{i} has the form (p,𝐜α,𝐀α,π)(p,{{\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}},\mathbf{A}_{\alpha},\pi) if PiP_{i} is a definition package and has the form Pi=(p,𝐀o,π)P_{i}=(p,\mathbf{A}_{o},\pi) if PiP_{i} is a theorem package. Define T0=TT_{0}=T and, for all ii with 0≤i≤n−10\leq i\leq n-1, define Ti+1=T⁡[Pi+1]T_{i+1}=T[P_{i+1}] if Pi+1P_{i+1} is a definition package and Ti+1=TiT_{i+1}=T_{i} if Pi+1P_{i+1} is a theorem package. In the former case, πi+1\pi_{i+1} is a proof that 𝐀α↓\mathbf{A}_{\alpha}{\downarrow} is valid in TiT_{i}, and in the latter case, πi+1\pi_{i+1} is a proof that 𝐀o\mathbf{A}_{o} is valid in TiT_{i}. These proofs may be either traditional or formal.

The validation proofs for the definitions and theorems of a development are not included in the modules we have used to construct developments and to transport definitions and theorems. Instead, we give in this appendix, for each of the definitions and theorems in the developments defined in Sections 2–10, a traditional proof that validates the definition or theorem. The proofs are almost entirely straightforward. The proofs reference some of the axioms, rules of inference, and metatheorems of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, the formal proof system for Alonzo presented in [20]. These are legitimate to use since 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is sound by the Soundness Theorem [20, Theorem 8.6 and Theorem B.11].

    Γ∪Δ\displaystyle\Gamma\cup\Delta ⊨(∏i=mng​i)⋅(∏i=mnh​i)≃(∏i=mn−1g​i)⋅g​n⋅(∏i=mn−1h​i)⋅h​n\displaystyle\vDash{{{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n}{g\,i}\Big)}\mathrel{\cdot}{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n}{h\,i}\Big)}}\simeq{{{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n-1}{g\,i}\Big)}\mathrel{\cdot}{g\,n}}\mathrel{\cdot}{{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n-1}{h\,i}\Big)}\mathrel{\cdot}{h\,n}}}} (2)

    (∏i=mn−1g​i)⋅(∏i=mn−1h​i)⋅g​n⋅h​n\displaystyle\phantom{{}\vDash{}}{{{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n-1}{g\,i}\Big)}\mathrel{\cdot}{\Big(\prod\limits_{{i}={m}}^{n-1}{h\,i}\Big)}}\mathrel{\cdot}{{g\,n}\mathrel{\cdot}{h\,n}}} (3)

    U{α}↓{U_{\{\alpha\}}{\downarrow}}.

The following lemma is an expanded version of [20, Lemma 13.9]:

Lemma B.2

Let Φ=(μ,ν)\Phi=(\mu,\nu) be a translation from T1T_{1} to T2T_{2}.

  1. 1.

    If α∈𝒯⁡(L1)\alpha\in{\cal T}(L_{1}) and μ¯​(α)∈𝒬2\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\in{\cal Q}_{2}, then T2⊨μ¯​(α)↓⇒ν¯​(U{α})=μ¯​(α)T_{2}\vDash{\overline{\mu}(\alpha){\downarrow}}\Rightarrow{{\overline{\nu}(U_{\{\alpha\}})}={\overline{\mu}(\alpha)}}.

  2. 2.

    If α∈𝒯⁡(L1)\alpha\in{\cal T}(L_{1}) and μ¯​(α)∈𝒬2\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\in{\cal Q}_{2}, then T2⊨μ¯​(α)↑⇒ν¯​(U{α})=∅{τ​(μ¯​(α))}T_{2}\vDash{\overline{\mu}(\alpha){\uparrow}}\Rightarrow{{\overline{\nu}(U_{\{\alpha\}})}={\emptyset_{\{\tau(\overline{\mu}(\alpha))\}}}}.

  3. 3.

    If 𝐚∈ℬ1\mathbf{a}\in{\cal B}_{1} and μ⁡(𝐚)∈𝒬2\mu(\mathbf{a})\in{\cal Q}_{2}, then

    T2⊨ν¯​(U{𝐚}≠∅{𝐚})⇔(μ⁡(𝐚)↓∧μ⁡(𝐚)≠∅{τ⁡(μ⁡(𝐚))}).T_{2}\vDash{\overline{\nu}({U_{\{\mathbf{a}\}}}\not={\emptyset_{\{\mathbf{a}\}}})}\Leftrightarrow{({\mu(\mathbf{a}){\downarrow}}\wedge{{\mu(\mathbf{a})}\not={\emptyset_{\{\tau(\mu(\mathbf{a}))\}}}})}.
  4. 4.

    If 𝐜α∈𝒞1{{\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}}\in{\cal C}_{1} and μ¯​(α)∈𝒯2\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\in{\cal T}_{2}, then T2⊨ν¯​(𝐜α↓U{α})⇔ν⁡(𝐜α)↓T_{2}\vDash{\overline{\nu}({{\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}}\downarrow{U_{\{\alpha\}}})}\Leftrightarrow{\nu({\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}){\downarrow}}.

  5. 5.

    If 𝐜α∈𝒞1{{\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}}\in{\cal C}_{1} and μ¯​(α)∈𝒬2\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\in{\cal Q}_{2}, then

    T2⊨μ¯​(α)↓⇒ν¯​(𝐜α↓U{α})⇔ν⁡(𝐜α)↓μ¯​(α).T_{2}\vDash{\overline{\mu}(\alpha){\downarrow}}\Rightarrow{{\overline{\nu}({{\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha}}\downarrow{U_{\{\alpha\}}})}\Leftrightarrow{{\nu({\mathbf{c}}_{\alpha})}\downarrow{\overline{\mu}(\alpha)}}}.

Proof Let α∈𝒯⁡(L1)\alpha\in{\cal T}(L_{1}), μ¯​(α)∈𝒬2\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\in{\cal Q}_{2}, and (⋆)(\star) MM be a general model of T2T_{2} in which μ¯​(α)↓{\overline{\mu}(\alpha){\downarrow}} is true. We must show that ν¯​(U{α})=μ¯​(α){{\overline{\nu}(U_{\{\alpha\}})}={\overline{\mu}(\alpha)}} is true in MM. Then

ν¯​(U{α})\displaystyle\phantom{{}\equiv{}}\overline{\nu}(U_{\{\alpha\}})
≡ν¯(λx:α.To)\displaystyle\equiv\overline{\nu}(\lambda\,x:\alpha\mathrel{.}T_{o})
≡λ​x:μ¯​(α).To\displaystyle\equiv\lambda\,x:\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\mathrel{.}T_{o}
≡λ​x:τ⁡(μ¯​(α)).(x∈μ¯​(α)↦To∣Fo).\displaystyle\equiv\lambda\,x:\tau(\overline{\mu}(\alpha))\mathrel{.}({x}\in{\overline{\mu}(\alpha)}\mapsto T_{o}\mid F_{o}).

by the definition of ν¯\overline{\nu} and notational definitions. The last expression is clearly equal to λ​x:τ⁡(μ¯​(α)).μ¯​(α)​x\lambda\,x:\tau(\overline{\mu}(\alpha))\mathrel{.}\overline{\mu}(\alpha)\,x, which is equal to μ¯​(α)\overline{\mu}(\alpha) in MM by (⋆)(\star). This proves part 1. Part 2 follows from the proof of part 1 and the notational definition for the empty set pseudoconstant. Part 3 follows immediately from the definition of ν¯\overline{\nu} and parts 1 and 2. Part 4 follows from the definition of ν¯\overline{\nu} and the notational definition for the defined-in-quasitype operator. And part 5 follows immediately from the definition of ν¯\overline{\nu} and part 1.  □\Box

Theorem B.3 (Existential Instantiation)

If Γ⊢𝔄𝐀o⇒𝐁o\Gamma\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\mathbf{A}_{o}}\Rightarrow{\mathbf{B}_{o}}}, then

Γ⊢𝔄(∃𝐱:α.𝐀o)⇒𝐁o,\Gamma\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{(\exists\,\mathbf{x}:\alpha\mathrel{.}\mathbf{A}_{o})}\Rightarrow{\mathbf{B}_{o}}},

provided that (𝐱:α){({\mathbf{x}}:{\alpha})} is not free in 𝐁o\mathbf{B}_{o} or in any member of Γ\Gamma.

Proof Let (⋆)(\star) (𝐱:α)({\mathbf{x}}:{\alpha}) be not free in 𝐁o\mathbf{B}_{o} or in any member of Γ\Gamma.

Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢𝔄𝐀o⇒𝐁o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\mathbf{A}_{o}}\Rightarrow{\mathbf{B}_{o}}} (1)
Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢¬𝔄⁡𝐁o⇒¬𝐀o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\neg{\mathbf{B}_{o}}}\Rightarrow{\neg{\mathbf{A}_{o}}}} (2)
Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢¬𝔄⁡𝐁o⇒∀𝐱:α.¬𝐀o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\neg{\mathbf{B}_{o}}}\Rightarrow{\forall\,\mathbf{x}:\alpha\mathrel{.}\neg{\mathbf{A}_{o}}}} (3)
Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢¬𝔄⁡𝐁o⇒¬¬∀⁡𝐱:α.¬𝐀o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\neg{\mathbf{B}_{o}}}\Rightarrow{\neg{\neg{\forall\,\mathbf{x}:\alpha\mathrel{.}\neg{\mathbf{A}_{o}}}}}} (4)
Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢¬𝔄⁡𝐁o⇒¬∃⁡𝐱:α.𝐀o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{\neg{\mathbf{B}_{o}}}\Rightarrow{\neg{\exists\,\mathbf{x}:\alpha\mathrel{.}\mathbf{A}_{o}}}} (5)
Γ\displaystyle\Gamma ⊢𝔄(∃𝐱:α.𝐀o)⇒𝐁o\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathfrak{A}}{{(\exists\,\mathbf{x}:\alpha\mathrel{.}\mathbf{A}_{o})}\Rightarrow{\mathbf{B}_{o}}} (6)

(1) is given; (2) follows from (1), (4) follows from (3), and (6) follows from (5) by the Tautology Rule [20, Corollary A.46]; (3) follows from (2) and (⋆)(\star) by [20, Lemma A.47] and (5) follows from (4) by the notational definition for ∃\exists. □\Box

Lemma B.4

Let TT be 𝖬𝖮𝖭\mathsf{MON} extended by the definition 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟤\mathsf{Def2}. The formula

AM⋅opBM≃BM⋅AM{{{\textbf{A}_{M}}\mathrel{\cdot^{\rm op}}{\textbf{B}_{M}}}\simeq{{\textbf{B}_{M}}\mathrel{\cdot}{\textbf{A}_{M}}}}

is valid in TT.

Proof Let Xo\textbf{X}_{o} be

AM⋅opBM≃BM⋅AM,{{{\textbf{A}_{M}}\mathrel{\cdot^{\rm op}}{\textbf{B}_{M}}}\simeq{{\textbf{B}_{M}}\mathrel{\cdot}{\textbf{A}_{M}}}},

NN be a model of TT, and φ∈𝖺𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇⁡(N)\varphi\in\mathsf{assign}(N). Suppose that VφN​(AM)V^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{A}_{M}) or VφN​(BM)V^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{B}_{M}) is undefined. Then clearly VφN​(Xo)=tV^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{X}_{o})=\mbox{{\sc t}}. Now suppose that VφN​(AM)V^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{A}_{M}) and VφN​(BM)V^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{B}_{M}) are defined. Then VφN​(Xo)=tV^{N}_{\varphi}(\textbf{X}_{o})=\mbox{{\sc t}} by 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝟤\mathsf{Def2}. □\Box
